Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah's blessings and peace be upon our Prophet Muhammad, his family, his companions, and those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment.

(...) on the tafsir (explanation) of this surah, as far as is made easy. It is the saying of the Blessed and Exalted: ﴿Woe to every scorner and mocker, who has gathered wealth and counted it. He thinks that his wealth will make him immortal. No! He will surely be thrown into the Crusher. And what will make you know what the Crusher is? It is the fire of Allah, kindled, which rises over the hearts. Indeed, it will be closed over them, in extended columns.﴾ [al-Humazah 1-9].

In this surah, Allah, glorified and exalted, begins with the word ﴿Woe﴾ (wayl), and it is a word of threat. That is, it indicates that a punishment is established for whoever has these attributes: ﴿scorner and mocker﴾, and so on to the end. It was also said that ﴿wayl﴾ is the name of a valley in Hell, but the first view is more sound.

﴿For every scorner and mocker﴾: ﴿kull﴾ (every) is among the forms of generality ('umum). ﴿Humazah﴾ and ﴿lumazah﴾ are two descriptive words for one described person. So, are they of one meaning, that is, do ﴿humazah﴾ and ﴿lumazah﴾ have the same meaning, or do they differ in meaning?

Some scholars said: they are two words for one meaning; that is, the humazah is the lumazah. Others said: rather, each of them has a meaning different from the other.

There is a principle (qa'idah) that I would like to point out in tafsir and beyond tafsir: when it is uncertain whether two words have the same meaning or each word has its own meaning, we follow the second; that is, we give each word a meaning. For if we make the two words have one meaning, this becomes a repetition for which there is no need. But if we give each word its own meaning, this becomes an establishing of a new meaning and a distinction between the two words. The correct view regarding this verse, ﴿every scorner and mocker﴾, is that there is a difference between them: ﴿hamz﴾ is by action, and ﴿lamz﴾ is by the tongue, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities. If they are given from them, they are satisfied; but if they are not given from them, at once they become angry.﴾ [at-Tawbah 58].

The hamz is by action; that is, he mocks people by his deeds: either by twisting his face, frowning, or the like, or by gesture, such as when he points at a person and says, "Look at him," in order to disparage him, or the like.

So, hamz is by what? By action. And lamz is by the tongue. That is, some people, may Allah protect us, are obsessed with finding fault in human beings: either by their deed, and he is the one who scorns (hammaz), or by their speech, and he is the one who defames (lammaz). This is like the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And do not obey every contemptible oath-swearer, a scorner, going about with slander﴾ [al-Qalam 10-11].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 104, verse 2:

﴿Who has gathered wealth and counted it.﴾ This is also among his ugly attributes: he is a jamma' manna' (one who hoards and withholds). He gathers wealth and withholds giving, so he is a miser who does not give. He gathers wealth and counts it (yu'addiduh).

It has been said: the meaning of at-ta'did (counting) is al-ihsa' (enumeration). That is, because of his intense attachment to wealth, each time he goes to the chest and counts, he counts the dirhams in the chest in the morning, and at the end of the day he counts them again, although he knows that he has taken nothing from it and added nothing to it. But because of the intensity of his attachment to wealth, he keeps returning to it and counting it. This is why the verb is in the intensive form ﴿'addadahu﴾, meaning he counted it repeatedly. Why? Because of the intensity of his attachment and love for it; he fears that it may have decreased, or he wants to be reassured by an increase over what came before. So he is always counting his wealth.

It has also been said: the meaning of ﴿'addadahu﴾ is that he made it a 'uddah (a reserve or means of preparation) for himself; that is, he saved it for the calamities of time. Although the wording may allow this, it is far-fetched, because preparing wealth for the calamities of time, while fulfilling what is obligatory by paying what is due on it of zakat and rights, is not blameworthy. What is blameworthy is that a person's greatest concern becomes wealth, that he keeps returning to it, counting it, and looking to see whether it has increased or decreased. Therefore, the view that the meaning of ﴿'addadahu﴾ is (...) is a weak opinion.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 104, verse 3:

﴿He thinks that his wealth will make him immortal.﴾ He means: this man thinks that his wealth will make him last forever and keep him alive, either in his body or in his remembrance. For a person's lifespan is not merely what remains of him in this world; rather, a person's lifespan in reality is what makes him endure after his death, so that his mention remains in people's hearts and on their tongues. So He says in this verse: ﴿He thinks that his wealth will make him immortal﴾, meaning: his mention will endure or his life will be prolonged. But the matter is not so, for people of wealth, if they are not known for generosity and giving, will indeed be made to endure, but through a bad remembrance. It is said: "More stingy than so-and-so," and "More stingy than so-and-so," and they are mentioned in gatherings and reproached.

Therefore He said: ﴿Nay, verily he will be thrown into the Huţamah (the Crusher).﴾ ﴿Nay﴾ here, the scholars call it a particle of restraint (ḥarf radʿ); that is, it restrains this speaker or this reckoner from his saying or from his reckoning. It may also carry the meaning of "truly," i.e., truly he will be thrown; and both are correct.

This man, his wealth will not make him immortal, nor will it make his remembrance immortal. Rather, he will be forgotten and his mention will be folded away, and he may even be mentioned with evil for not fulfilling what Allah obligated upon him of spending.

﴿He will surely be thrown into the Huţamah.﴾ This lam falls in the answer to an implied oath, and the sense is: "By Allah, he will surely be thrown into the Huţamah," that is, he will be cast down with force. When we say that the lam is in answer to an oath, the sentence is emphasized by the lam, the energetic nūn (nūn al-tawkīd), and the implied oath. Such usage is frequent in the Noble Qur'an; that is, emphasizing a matter by an oath, the lam and the nūn is something common in the Qur'an, and Allah, exalted is He, swears by a thing to affirm it and to magnify its status.

As for His saying ﴿he will be thrown (la-yunbadhanna)﴾, what is it that is thrown? Is it the owner of the wealth or the wealth? We may say: both are thrown. As for the owner of the wealth, Allah says in another verse: ﴿On the Day they will be pushed toward the Fire of Hell with a violent pushing﴾ [al-Tur 13]. They will be pushed and trampled by hands, or by whatever Allah wills. And here He says "yunbadh," that is, cast down.

﴿Into the Huṭamah﴾. The Huṭamah is that which crushes a thing, that is, it breaks it into pieces and shatters it. So what is it?

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And what will make you know what the Huṭamah is?﴾ This form is for magnification and glorification.

﴿It is the Fire of Allah, kindled﴾. This is the answer: that is, it is the kindled Fire of Allah. Allah, glorified and exalted, attributed it to Himself because He punishes with it whoever deserves punishment. So it is a punishment of justice, not a punishment of injustice; that is, a fire with which Allah burns whoever deserves to be punished with it. Thus it is a fire of justice, not a fire of injustice, because burning with fire may be injustice or may be justice. The punishment of the disbelievers with the Fire is undoubtedly justice, and the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, is praised for it, since He dealt with these people according to what they deserve.

Consider His saying (Huṭamah) together with the form of this doer: (Humazah), (Lumazah), (Huṭamah) are of one pattern, so that the recompense corresponds to the deed even in the wording.

﴿The Fire of Allah, kindled﴾, that is: the blazing, the set ablaze.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 104, verse 7:

﴿The fire which mounts over the hearts.﴾ ﴿Al-af'idah (the hearts)⦆ is the plural of fu'ad, which is the heart. The meaning is that it (the fire) reaches the hearts, — may Allah protect us — because of its intense heat, even though the hearts are concealed within the chests, and between them and the outer skin lie the layers that lie between them. Yet despite that, this fire reaches the hearts.

Verse 8: "Indeed, it [i.e., al-Hutamah], which is the fire of Allah kindled, will be closed over them" — over whom? Over the backbiter, the slanderer, the one who gathers wealth and counts it, the one who withholds good. He did not say "closed over him," even though the referent is singular; the pronoun is returned in plural form in terms of meaning, because "every backbiter and slanderer" (li-kulli humazatin lumazatin) is general and includes all backbiters and all slanderers.

"Indeed, it is closed over them": i.e., shut, its doors locked, with no hope of relief for them, and Allah forbid. "Every time they wish to get out of it, they are returned to it" (al-Sajdah 20): that is, they are raised up to its doors so that they hope to get out, and then afterward they are overturned back into it and returned to it. All of this is for the severity of the punishment, because when a person hopes for relief and that he will be saved and freed, he rejoices; when he is sent back, it becomes a fresh reversal, and Allah forbid. Thus they are punished in their consciences and their bodies. The punishment of the people of the Fire is described in detail in the noble Qur'an and the Prophetic Sunnah.

"Indeed, it is closed over them": locked. Now consider: suppose a person were, for example, in a room or in a car in which fires had blazed and there was no exit, the doors locked. What would that be? A great regret that nothing could equal. They, Allah forbid, are thus in the Fire; the Fire is closed over them.

In vows of extended pillars (fi ʿamadin mumaddadah). That is: this Fire is closed shut, and upon it are extended pillars; meaning, just as we say, "great locks," so that no one attempts to open it.

﴿فِي عَمَدٍ مُمَدَّدَةٍ﴾ meaning: extended over all the sides and corners, so that no one is able to open it or get out of it.

God, glorified and exalted, related this to us and explained it to us not merely so that we recite it with our tongues or know its meaning with our understanding, but the purpose is that we beware of it, that we beware of these blameworthy traits: defaming people by speech, defaming people by deed, and greed for wealth, to the point that it is as if a person was created only for wealth, to be immortalized by it, or as if wealth is immortalized for him. We know that whoever has this condition, his recompense is this Fire, which is, as God described it: ﴿الْحُطَمَةُ﴾ (the Crusher), ﴿تَطَّلِعُ عَلَى الْأَفْئِدَةِ﴾ (it rises over the hearts), ﴿مُوصَدَةٌ﴾ (closed shut), ﴿فِي عَمَدٍ مُمَدَّدَةٍ﴾ (in extended pillars). We ask God, exalted is He, to protect us and you from it, and to grant us sincerity in speech and deed and steadfastness upon His religion.
